title: You're not failing at product transformation. You're playing the wrong game.
author: Leading in Product
summary: Product transformation frameworks and playbooks were written for companies that already had some product culture baked in—organizations where the soil was prepared, leadership was committed, and resources were dedicated. Most practitioners are applying those frameworks in companies without those preconditions, which is why the advice fails: it is a perfectly good recipe made in the wrong kitchen. The article argues that what most product leaders are actually doing is trying to drive a company-wide culture shift from inside a single function, without executive authority, dedicated budget, or an organizational mandate—one of the hardest things you can attempt inside a large organization. The path forward is to shrink ambition deliberately: pick one team, give them clarity and space, bake the new culture into everyday decisions rather than announcements. Quiet and consistent proof is more powerful than loud programs with slide decks. Trust people before they have earned it, because the transformation needs them more than it needs to be right. When a team delivers better outcomes and treats customers like real people, it becomes a reference point inside the organization—and reference points spread without programs.
points: Product transformation playbooks were written for companies that already had product culture; applying them in organizations without those preconditions is a recipe for failure

You’ve read the books, done the conferences, and you genuinely know what good product work looks like.
And somewhere in the back of your mind, quietly, a question has been growing: is it me?
But the honest answer is more uncomfortable than simple reassurance.
Stephanie Leue, a respected voice in product leadership, put it plainly: you’re not doing it wrong.
And until you understand which game you’re actually in, no amount of effort, good intentions, or borrowed frameworks will get you where you want to go.
The advice wasn’t written for you Pick up almost any book on product transformation and you’ll find the same story told in slightly different words.
But those conditions are almost never named, because the people writing those books didn’t have to think about them.
